  <section v="0">
    <sectionSummaryBrief>This section contains the opening header for the maamar on Purim of the year 5711.</sectionSummaryBrief>
    <t s="0">With the help of Heaven.</t>
    <t s="1">Purim,</t>
    <t s="2">[5]711*</t>
  </section>
  <section v="1">
    <sectionSummaryBrief>This section discusses the puzzling acceptance of the Torah by the Jews in the time of Haman, explaining that it required the service of self-nullification (Mesiras Nefesh) throughout the year.</sectionSummaryBrief>
    <t s="0">"And the Jews accepted that which they had already undertaken, etc." And the Rebbe asks: it is astonishing, etc. And in the time of exile, etc., and particularly in the time of Haman when the decree was, etc., and specifically then they fulfilled what they had already accepted.</t>
    <t s="1">And he answers: that then they were in a state of Mesiras Nefesh (self-sacrifice) the entire year.</t>
    <t s="2">And behold, why was it specifically necessary to have service in Mesiras Nefesh in order to fulfill that which they had already begun?</t>
    <t s="3">One must preface an explanation of the matter of "that which they had already begun," which refers to the time of the Giving of the Torah (Matan Torah),</t>
    <t s="4">For the innovation at the Giving of the Torah was, as is known, the giving of the Torah and mitzvos specifically in physicality,</t>
    <t s="5">Meaning to nullify the decree that "the Romans shall not descend, etc.,"</t>
    <t s="6">And therefore they were given specifically to souls in bodies, in their union together.</t>
    <t s="7">And also in Torah and mitzvos there must be a union of the physical aspect within them and the spirituality,</t>
    <t s="8">Meaning that one makes it a mitzvah,</t>
    <t s="9">And this too is only after refinement in exile.</t>
    <t s="10">And therefore, also in the fulfillment of Torah and mitzvos there are several modes,</t>
    <t s="11">The first: one who performs Torah and mitzvos as "the commandments of men learned by rote," without vitality, or not for its own sake, with the motive that they will make him a rabbi and the like, which is not vitality,</t>
    <t s="12">Or out of fear of G-d, which is not vitality but rather the opposite—contraction and constriction.</t>
    <t s="13">The second: one who does the above out of love for Hashem with great vitality, which comes from his soul that spreads forth and overcomes,</t>
    <t s="14">Which generally includes service out of nature, or habit that has become nature, or service according to the intellect and understanding,</t>
    <t s="15">And there is also that which is above intellect and understanding, which is not an independent entity, but rather he desires to fulfill the will of the Creator.</t>
    <t s="16">And corresponding to these distinctions, there are also distinctions within the Torah itself.</t>
    <t s="17">Torah in order to know the deed,</t>
    <t s="18">For this is specifically the purpose,</t>
    <t s="19">And consequently there are limitations within it,</t>
    <t s="20">The law of a holiday on its holiday, and the like,</t>
    <t s="21">And specifically "in the four [orders] we teach."</t>
    <t s="22">The study of Torah for its own sake, wherein "he will delight in her love constantly" because of her intrinsic virtue, at least according to intellect and understanding.</t>
    <t s="23">And above the aforementioned: [study] for its own sake truly, for the sake of the Torah,</t>
    <t s="24">Meaning above intellect and understanding,</t>
    <t s="25">For then he also connects the Torah that issues from wisdom to its source in the Holy One, blessed be He.</t>
    <t s="26">And through what can this be? This too is by one showing in himself that he is in a state of Mesiras Nefesh.</t>
    <t s="27">And there must always be a connection of the Torah to its source,</t>
    <t s="28">For ostensibly, one could say</t>
  </section>
